stances.claim: PH 6.5% growth for first nine months of 2012 gives reason to smile but not yet to celebrate -- sustainable, inclusive growth benefiting middle class and poor, not just entrepreneurs, is the real test.

Critics who attribute growth entirely to OFW/BPO are partly right but cannot ignore business morale, record stock market, revenue rises, and ratings upgrades, nor the CCT program wisely continued from Arroyo.

stances.claim: The Acemoglu-Robinson inclusive-vs-extractive institutions framework, Filipinized, requires: level playing field, property rights, innovation tolerance, zero corruption/nepotism/cronyism, transparency, accountability, rule of law.
The Asian crisis of the 1990s -- which threw PH back when it was so close to Tiger Economy status -- is the cautionary precedent warning against complacency in 2012.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban surveys the Philippines' remarkable 2012 economic performance -- 6.3% GDP growth in Q1, 6% in Q2, and 7.1% in Q3, for an overall 6.5% in the first nine months, making it the best performer in ASEAN and second only to China in Asia -- noting IMF chief Christine Lagarde's hailing of PH as the only country where the IMF raised its growth forecast. He credits Arroyo's administration for the 2006 graduation from IMF borrower to lender, and the Aquino economic team for continuing and expanding the Conditional Cash Transfer program. He rebuts critics who attribute growth solely to OFW and BPO workers by pointing to high business morale, record stock market performance, rising revenues, and ratings upgrades. He frames the core challenge using the World Bank-sent book 'Why Nations Fail' by Acemoglu and Robinson: inclusive institutions (property rights, level playing field, innovation incentives) vs extractive ones -- 'Filipinized' as zero corruption/nepotism/cronyism plus transparency, accountability, and rule of law. He closes with BPI president Montinola's caution: 'seeing the peak is very different from scaling the peak,' recalling how PH was 'so close in the mid-90s before the Asian crises threw us back to earth.' Reason to smile, but not yet to celebrate.
